Pooled Heterogeneity for brma Objects

Source: R/wrappers.R
pooled_heterogeneity.brma.Rd

Computes heterogeneity (tau) of a fitted brma object at the average fitted scale design (the mean of the observation-specific tau) and, for random-formula models, at the average expanded random-effect design.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'brma'
pooled_heterogeneity(
  object,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.975),
  conditional = FALSE,
  component = "all",
  ...
)

Arguments

object

a fitted brma object

probs

quantiles of the posterior distribution to be displayed. Defaults to c(.025, .975) for 95% credible intervals.

conditional

whether to return the pooled heterogeneity conditional on the heterogeneity component for RoBMA product-space objects. Defaults to FALSE.

component

heterogeneity component to return for brma.mv() models. Defaults to "all". Use "total" for the variance-additive total heterogeneity.

...

additional arguments passed to predict.brma (as_measure, V_new, and conditioning_depth); wrapper arguments such as newdata, type, and quiet are fixed (supplying one is R's error for an argument matched twice, as for predict()), and other unknown arguments are unused and trigger a warning.

Value

A brma_samples object containing posterior samples. When printed, displays a summary table. For decomposed brma.mv() models, a named list of brma_samples objects is returned. Use summary() on an individual object (as.data.frame() of an individual object returns its draws) or as.data.frame() on the complete result to obtain a summary data frame with component and parameter identifiers. Use as.data.frame(format = "list") to retain separate component tables. The samples can be converted to posterior draws formats using as_draws().

Details

For location-scale models, the function returns the arithmetic mean over the fitted rows of the observation-specific tau, as in 4.0.0; it equals rowMeans(predict(object, type = "terms.scale")). It is not the root mean square heterogeneity across the observed rows. Use summary_heterogeneity() for the latter.

For models without scale regression, this returns the single tau parameter.

For multilevel (3-level) models, the returned tau is the total heterogeneity: tau = sqrt(tau_within^2 + tau_between^2).

For brma.mv() models, one ordinary selected component is named tau; a genuine variance-additive total is named tau_total; and a mean-variance allocation anchor is named tau_common. These quantities are available when a random formula is declared. For random-formula models, component = "all" returns one brma_samples object when there is a single heterogeneity component and a named list when there are multiple components. component = "total" computes the variance-additive total at the average random-effect design. Random slopes are evaluated as \(\bar q^T G \bar q\), including within-block correlations. Default and named allocation components retain their declared scale anchors; explicit totals and pooled-effect prediction intervals use the full covariance of the average design, including allocation-owned blocks. With a known group covariance \(R\), the reported sd is the fitted multiplier of that kernel. It need not equal every row's marginal standard deviation when \(\mathrm{diag}(R)\) is not one. Row-specific marginal standard deviations are available from predict(type = "terms.scale"). A scale formula of a random-formula model enters the average random-effect design as the arithmetic mean of the observation-specific tau, as for the univariate models. predict(object, newdata = TRUE, type = "terms.scale") returns the same component result: a named list for several components and one brma_samples object for a single component.

For brma.mv() models and models with factor-specific or random-slope terms, the average expanded random-effect design can be synthetic and need not correspond to a single realizable outcome or study. The result is the heterogeneity of that linear composite, not typical heterogeneity across the observed designs. Interpret it only when the composite has a meaningful scientific interpretation; use summary_heterogeneity() for observed-design heterogeneity or predict(..., newdata = ...) for a specified realizable design.

See also

predict.brma(), pooled_effect(), blup()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
if (requireNamespace("metadat", quietly = TRUE)) {
  data(dat.lehmann2018, package = "metadat")
  fit <- brma(
    yi      = yi,
    vi      = vi,
    data    = dat.lehmann2018,
    measure = "SMD",
    seed    = 1,
    silent  = TRUE
  )

  pooled_heterogeneity(fit)
}
} # }
